key_insight: Scaling automated discovery with LLM agents does not keep improving forever: once agents accumulate too much history, performance plateaus. The paper’s core takeaway is that progress often requires selective forgetting, not just more iteration, more agents, or more communication.
problem_solved: The paper addresses how to scale automated research systems powered by LLM agents without hitting diminishing returns. It asks why longer runs, parallel agents, and agent collaboration eventually stop producing better discoveries.
method: Study three scaling strategies for automated research: longer single-agent iteration, parallel agents, and communicating agent swarms.
Use iterative refinement with scored verifiers to evaluate discovery quality over time.
Analyze how accumulating history affects search behavior and show that removing or forgetting past context can help agents continue making progress.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners building agentic research systems, this suggests that memory management is as important as compute scaling. Designing systems that prune stale context or reset search history may unlock better long-horizon discovery.
visual_elements: A plateau curve showing discovery quality vs. more iterations/agents
A pipeline diagram comparing single-agent, parallel-agent, and collaborative-agent scaling
An icon-based memory stack with a 'forget' or pruning symbol
A before/after illustration of full history vs. selective context retention
paper_authors: Shangyin Tan, Ben Zhou, Lakshya A Agrawal, Jialin Zhang, Yilin Chen
